chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ali ibn al-Sindi, from Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Sa'id, from al-Karam, from Maysar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) was asked: 'How much is there between the truth and falsehood?' He replied: 'Four fingers.' The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) placed his hand on his ear and his eyes and said: 'What your eyes see is the truth, and what your ears hear is mostly falsehood.'

key_terms.أَرْبَعُ أَصَابِعَ: Four fingers (metaphor for a short distance)
key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (title for Imam Ali)

ai.seo_question: What is the distance between truth and falsehood according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Khisal*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) uses the metaphor of 'four fingers' to illustrate the narrow margin separating truth from falsehood, linking sensory perception to spiritual discernment. While visual perception is often associated with clarity and direct evidence, auditory perception is highlighted as susceptible to deception and hearsay, a concept deeply rooted in Shia epistemology regarding the reliability of witnesses and divine signs. This teaching underscores the necessity of critical evaluation of what is heard against the clarity of what is seen, reflecting the broader Islamic emphasis on verifying information before acceptance.
